about.text: The explainer map (FAL-935): one node per explainer across AA SL, AA HL, AI SL and AI HL. An explainer is a short narrated clip that teaches one idea, at the grain of a Relic lesson (lessons.json). Prerequisites are what a student should have seen first and what a tutor calls back to; they suggest and never lock, and every prerequisite is in every course of the explainer that needs it. Where AA and AI handle an idea differently there is one shared core explainer plus a method explainer per course built on it; HL extensions build on the SL explainer. Check and regenerate with node tools/explainers.mjs; see EXPLAINERS.md.

fields.id: ex.<zone>.<slug>. The slug is the lessons.json slug where the explainer has a lesson. Permanent once on main.
fields.title: What the student sees.
fields.zone: The map zone and so the tutor who narrates it (tools/explainer-clips/teachers.json): foundations, algebra, functions, geometry, stats or calculus. Not foundations: the zone's syllabus topic is the topic of at least one of its subtopics.
fields.cluster: The part of the island it belongs to; EXPLAINERS.md draws one diagram per cluster.
fields.idea: One sentence: what the explainer teaches.
fields.layer: Computed by --write from courses: core, aa-ai-hl, aa-hl-ai, aa, ai, hl, aa-hl or ai-hl (tools/explainers.mjs, LAYERS).
fields.courses: The courses that get it: a subset of aa-sl, aa-hl, ai-sl, ai-hl. An SL course brings its HL course, and every course is a course of at least one of its subtopics.
fields.subtopics: Syllabus subtopic ids from aa-sl.json, aa-hl.json and ai.json. Foundations explainers list the subtopics they prepare for and do not count towards coverage.
fields.skills: Skill ids it teaches, each from one of its subtopics. Foundations explainers teach prior learning and list none.
fields.prereqs: Explainers to have seen first: the "this builds on" links. Each is in every course of this explainer. Where the explainer has a lesson, the lesson's prerequisites are reached through these whenever the courses allow.
fields.related: Explainers worth a "remember when" callback that are not prerequisites; each shares a course with this one.
fields.methods: The distinct approaches that each need their own worked example, as slugs; empty when there is one approach.
fields.lesson: The lessons.json id, when a Relic lesson teaches the same idea.
fields.question_types: Computed by --write: the question-types.json ids it prepares for, the types that share a skill with it plus its lesson's supports.
fields.threads: Computed by --write: the concept threads (threads.json) its skills belong to.
fields.priority: Computed by --write: { parts, rank }. parts is its weighted AA SL exam parts; rank is its place in the build order (EXPLAINERS.md, "Build order").
fields.note: Optional: why a judgment call about sharing or splitting was made.

explainers.title: Brackets Round Negatives
explainers.idea: Substitute a value into an expression by putting it in brackets, so a negative input is squared or multiplied correctly.

explainers.title: Keep the Scales Level
explainers.idea: Solve a linear equation by doing the same thing to both sides until the unknown stands alone.

explainers.title: Make It the Subject
explainers.idea: Rearrange a formula to make another letter the subject by undoing its operations in reverse order.

explainers.title: Two Lamps, One Point
explainers.idea: Solve two linear equations together by substitution or elimination, and read the answer as the point where two lines cross.

explainers.title: The Tipping See-Saw
explainers.idea: Solve a linear inequality like an equation, flipping the sign whenever both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative.

explainers.title: Fill the Rectangle
explainers.idea: Expand brackets by multiplying every term in one bracket by every term in the other, as the areas of a split rectangle.

explainers.title: Find the Sides
explainers.idea: Factorise a quadratic by finding the two brackets whose product it is, undoing expansion.

explainers.title: Roots That Split
explainers.idea: Simplify a surd by taking out square factors, so answers like √48 become 4√3.

explainers.title: Never Divide by Zero
explainers.idea: Simplify an algebraic fraction by cancelling common factors, never terms, and note the values that make the denominator zero.

explainers.title: One Multiplication
explainers.idea: Turn a percentage increase or decrease into a single multiplier, so a 4% rise is ×1.04 and a 4% fall is ×0.96.

explainers.title: Read the Gauge
explainers.idea: Read values from a scale, a table or a GDC screen and round them to three significant figures only at the end.

explainers.title: The Square on the Long Side
explainers.idea: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

explainers.title: Halfway and How Far
explainers.idea: Find the midpoint of two points by averaging their coordinates and the distance between them with Pythagoras.

explainers.title: Cross-Section Times Length
explainers.idea: Find the area of basic shapes and the volume of a prism or cylinder as cross-section area times length.

explainers.title: Powers of Ten
explainers.idea: Write a number as a × 10^k with 1 ≤ a < 10, so very large and very small quantities can be compared at a glance.

explainers.title: Calculating in Standard Form
explainers.idea: Multiply and divide numbers in standard form by handling the a parts and the powers of ten separately, then tidy the result back into standard form.

explainers.title: Sensible Accuracy
explainers.idea: Round to decimal places or significant figures that suit the data and the context, and check an answer against a quick estimate.

explainers.title: Bounds and Percentage Error
explainers.idea: A rounded measurement lies between half a unit below and half a unit above, and the percentage error compares the error with the exact value.

explainers.title: Add the Same Each Step
explainers.idea: An arithmetic sequence adds the common difference d at every step, so u_n = u₁ + (n − 1)d.
explainers.note: Teaches the nth term only, as pilot 1 does (FAL-952); working back from given terms is ex.algebra.arithmetic-from-terms.

explainers.title: Working Back from the Terms
explainers.idea: Set uₙ = u₁ + (n − 1)d equal to the terms you are given and solve for the missing u₁, d or n, counting the gaps between terms rather than the terms.
explainers.note: Split from ex.algebra.arithmetic-sequence so each script stays under 8 minutes (FAL-952). Two given terms need simultaneous equations; one term and its value need only the balance.

explainers.title: Adding Up an Arithmetic Sequence
explainers.idea: The sum of an arithmetic sequence is the number of terms times the average of the first and last terms.
explainers.note: Teaches the sum only, as pilot 2 does (FAL-952); the two forms of the formula are its two methods, and the GDC routes belong in a method explainer. Finding an unknown from a sum is ex.algebra.arithmetic-sum-unknown.

explainers.title: Working Back from a Sum
explainers.idea: Put what you know into the sum formula and solve for the unknown: a quadratic in n when the number of terms is missing, or linear equations in u₁ and d when n is known.
explainers.note: Split from ex.algebra.arithmetic-series (FAL-952). The quadratic in n is solved on the GDC (ex.functions.gdc-solve) because the by-hand quadratic formula is AA only; two given sums need simultaneous equations.

explainers.title: Sigma Notation
explainers.idea: Σ is an instruction to substitute each value of the counter in turn and add the results.

explainers.title: Constant Change in Context
explainers.idea: A quantity that changes by the same amount each period is an arithmetic sequence, and the question decides whether you want a term or a sum.

explainers.title: Multiply the Same Each Step
explainers.idea: A geometric sequence multiplies by the common ratio r at every step, so u_n = u₁r^(n − 1).
explainers.note: Teaches the nth term only, like ex.algebra.arithmetic-sequence (FAL-952); working back to r, u₁ or n is ex.algebra.geometric-from-terms.

explainers.title: Adding Up a Geometric Sequence
explainers.idea: The sum of a geometric sequence comes from subtracting r times the sum from the sum, which leaves only the first and last pieces.

explainers.title: Working Back to r and n
explainers.idea: Divide one given term by another so u₁ cancels and leaves a power of r, then find n for a given term or sum with logarithms or a GDC table.
explainers.note: Split from ex.algebra.geometric-sequence, the same split as the arithmetic pair (FAL-952). It comes after the series because SL1.3.find-n includes the least n with Sₙ above a target. Solving with logarithms (ex.functions.solve-with-logs) is not in AI SL, so there the GDC table is the method.

explainers.title: When a Sum Settles Down
explainers.idea: An infinite geometric series has a finite sum only when |r| < 1, because then each new term is too small to push the total past a limit.

explainers.title: The Sum to Infinity
explainers.idea: When |r| < 1 the infinite sum is u₁/(1 − r), and an equation in that formula finds a missing term or ratio.

explainers.title: Interest on Interest
explainers.idea: Compound interest multiplies the balance by the same factor every period, so it is a geometric sequence in money.

explainers.title: Losing Value
explainers.idea: Depreciation multiplies by a factor below 1, and inflation shrinks what money is really worth, so compare options in today's money.

explainers.title: Paying Off a Loan
explainers.idea: A loan is paid off by equal instalments while interest keeps growing the balance, and the TVM solver balances the two.

explainers.title: Saving Up and Paying Out
explainers.idea: An annuity is the same regular payment in or out of an account that earns compound interest, solved with the same TVM inputs as a loan.

explainers.title: Powers Follow Laws
explainers.idea: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, dividing subtracts them, a⁰ = 1 and a negative power is a reciprocal.

explainers.title: Fractional Powers Are Roots
explainers.idea: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, so a^(m/n) is a root and a power together, and the same laws still hold.

explainers.title: The Laws of Logarithms
explainers.idea: Because logs are exponents, the log of a product is a sum, the log of a quotient is a difference and the log of a power brings the power down.

explainers.title: Change of Base
explainers.idea: Any logarithm can be rewritten in another base as log_b a = log_c a / log_c b, which turns unfamiliar bases into ones you can handle.

explainers.title: Same Base, Same Power
explainers.idea: When both sides of an exponential equation can be written as powers of the same base, the exponents must be equal.

explainers.title: Solving Log Equations
explainers.idea: Combine the logs into a single log, rewrite it as a power, solve, then reject any answer that would take the log of a non-positive number.

explainers.title: Left Side to Right Side
explainers.idea: Prove an identity by starting from one side and rewriting it step by step until it becomes the other, never working on both at once.

explainers.title: Proofs About Whole Numbers
explainers.idea: Write a general even, odd or consecutive integer in algebra, such as 2n or 2n + 1, and the proof becomes a short expansion.

explainers.title: True for Every x
explainers.idea: When two expressions are equal for every x, their coefficients of each power of x must match, which finds unknown constants.

explainers.title: Proof by Induction
explainers.idea: Show a statement is true for the first case and that truth for k forces truth for k + 1, and it holds for every case like toppling dominoes.

explainers.title: Induction Beyond Series
explainers.idea: The same induction step proves divisibility, inequalities and derivative patterns, by writing the k + 1 case in terms of the k case.

explainers.title: Proof by Contradiction
explainers.idea: Assume the opposite of what you want, follow the logic to something impossible, and the assumption must be false.

explainers.title: One Counterexample Is Enough
explainers.idea: A single case where a claim fails disproves it, however many cases it works for.

explainers.title: Pascal's Triangle and nCr
explainers.idea: Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it and equals nCr, the number of ways to choose r items from n.

explainers.title: Expanding (a + b)^n
explainers.idea: The terms of (a + b)^n are nCr a^(n − r) b^r, so the coefficients come straight from a row of Pascal's triangle.

explainers.title: One Term of an Expansion
explainers.idea: Write the general term, set its power of x to the one you want, and the term follows without expanding everything.

explainers.title: Multiply the Choices
explainers.idea: When choices are made one after another, multiply the number of options at each stage; when they are alternatives, add.

explainers.title: Order Matters, or It Doesn't
explainers.idea: Permutations count arrangements where order matters and combinations count selections where it does not, so nPr = nCr × r!.

explainers.title: Binomial Series for Any Power
explainers.idea: For a fractional or negative power, (1 + x)^n becomes an infinite series that converges only when |x| < 1, and its first terms approximate the value.

explainers.title: Split the Fraction
explainers.idea: A fraction with a factorised denominator splits into simpler fractions, one per factor, found by substituting roots or comparing coefficients.

explainers.title: Systems on the GDC
explainers.idea: Write each condition as a linear equation in the unknowns and let the GDC solve the system, including finding a curve through given points.

explainers.title: Elimination by Hand
explainers.idea: Eliminate one unknown at a time from three equations until one equation in one unknown remains, then substitute back.

explainers.title: One, None or Infinitely Many
explainers.idea: A system has a unique solution, none or infinitely many, and when there are infinitely many the general solution uses a parameter.

explainers.title: Polynomial Roots on the GDC
explainers.idea: The polynomial solver gives every real root of a polynomial equation, and the context decides which roots make sense.

explainers.title: The Number i
explainers.idea: With i² = −1, complex numbers a + bi add and multiply like brackets, and dividing uses the conjugate to make the denominator real.

explainers.title: The Argand Diagram
explainers.idea: A complex number is a point on the Argand diagram, with its modulus as the distance from 0 and its argument as the angle from the positive real axis.

explainers.title: Equate Real and Imaginary Parts
explainers.idea: Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts and their imaginary parts are both equal, which turns one equation into two.

explainers.title: Roots Below the Axis
explainers.idea: A quadratic with a negative discriminant has two complex roots that are conjugates of each other.

explainers.title: Modulus and Argument Form
explainers.idea: The same complex number can be written as a + bi, as r cis θ or as re^(iθ), and each form makes different calculations easy.

explainers.title: Multiply Means Rotate and Stretch
explainers.idea: Multiplying complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments, so on the Argand diagram it is a stretch and a rotation.

explainers.title: Sums in Euler Form
explainers.idea: Adding or factorising numbers in Euler form, such as e^(iθ) + 1, reveals exact trigonometric values and identities.

explainers.title: Adding Waves with Complex Numbers
explainers.idea: Two waves of the same frequency add to one wave, whose amplitude and phase come from adding the matching complex numbers.

explainers.title: De Moivre's Theorem
explainers.idea: Raising r cis θ to the power n gives rⁿ cis nθ, so powers of complex numbers are quick in polar form.

explainers.title: Proving De Moivre
explainers.idea: De Moivre's theorem for positive integers follows by induction using the compound angle formulae.

explainers.title: Multiple-Angle Identities
explainers.idea: Expanding (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ by the binomial theorem and comparing with cos nθ + i sin nθ gives identities for cos nθ and sin nθ.

explainers.title: The nth Roots
explainers.idea: A complex number has n distinct nth roots, equally spaced round a circle on the Argand diagram.

explainers.title: Conjugate Root Pairs
explainers.idea: A polynomial with real coefficients has its complex roots in conjugate pairs, so knowing one root gives a quadratic factor.

explainers.title: Matrices and Multiplication
explainers.idea: A matrix is a table of numbers that adds entry by entry and multiplies row by column, and order matters because AB need not equal BA.

explainers.title: Undoing a Matrix
explainers.idea: A matrix with a non-zero determinant has an inverse that undoes it, so AX = B is solved by X = A⁻¹B.

explainers.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
explainers.idea: An eigenvector keeps its direction when the matrix acts on it and is only scaled by its eigenvalue, found from det(A − λI) = 0.

explainers.title: Diagonalising for Powers
explainers.idea: Writing A = PDP⁻¹ with the eigenvalues in D makes Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹, which predicts the long-run behaviour of a model.

explainers.title: Rise per Step
explainers.idea: The gradient of a line is the change in y for each step of 1 in x, the same everywhere along the line.

explainers.title: Pin and Swing
explainers.idea: One point and a gradient pin down a line, written as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), y = mx + c or ax + by + d = 0.

explainers.title: The Quarter Turn
explainers.idea: Parallel lines share a gradient, and perpendicular gradients multiply to −1 because a quarter turn swaps rise and run and flips a sign.

explainers.title: Start Plus Rate
explainers.idea: A linear model is a starting value plus a constant rate, so the intercept and the gradient each mean something in context.

explainers.title: One In, One Out
explainers.idea: A function takes each input to exactly one output, and f(3) means the output when the input is 3.

explainers.title: One Button, One Token
explainers.idea: A relation is a function when every input has exactly one output, which the vertical line test checks on a graph.

explainers.title: What Goes In, What Comes Out
explainers.idea: The domain is the set of inputs a function accepts and the range is the set of outputs it can produce.

explainers.title: Run It Backwards
explainers.idea: An inverse function undoes the original, taking each output back to the input that made it.

explainers.title: The Mirror Line
explainers.idea: The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the original in the line y = x, because inputs and outputs swap.

explainers.title: Two Machines in a Row
explainers.idea: A composite function f(g(x)) feeds the output of g into f, so the function nearest x acts first.

explainers.title: Rewire the Machine
explainers.idea: To find an inverse algebraically, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and make y the subject.

explainers.title: Cut It to Undo It
explainers.idea: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one, so restrict its domain, and the domain and range swap for the inverse.

explainers.title: How High, and Where?
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: A graph shows its highest and lowest points and its intercepts, and the GDC finds them to three significant figures.

explainers.title: Where the Tracks Cross
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: Where two graphs cross, their equations are both true, so solving f(x) = g(x) and finding the intersection are the same job.

explainers.title: Sweep the Beam
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: The number of solutions of f(x) = k is the number of times the horizontal line y = k meets the graph.

explainers.title: When Algebra Jams
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: When an equation has no algebraic method, graph both sides on the GDC and read off the intersections.

explainers.title: Spot the Impostor
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: A sketch shows the shape and the key features, labelled intercepts, turning points and asymptotes, over the right domain.

explainers.title: Stack the Heights
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: The graph of f + g adds the heights of the two graphs at each x, and f − g measures the gap between them.

explainers.title: Above the Line
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: f(x) > g(x) wherever the graph of f is above the graph of g, so the intersections mark where the answer changes.

explainers.title: Does It Make Sense?
explainers.cluster: Lines meet curves: graphs and the GDC
explainers.idea: After solving a model, keep only the answers that fit the domain and the story, and state them in its units.

explainers.title: Either Valve Shuts It
explainers.idea: If a product is zero, one of its factors is zero, so the roots of a(x − p)(x − q) = 0 are p and q.

explainers.title: The Fountain's Mirror
explainers.idea: A parabola is symmetric about a vertical line through its vertex, halfway between any two points at the same height.
explainers.note: Shared by all four courses, so it cannot require zero-product (AA only); AA students meet zero-product through vertex-form and quadratic-formula.

explainers.title: The Crane Hook
explainers.idea: In y = a(x − h)² + k the vertex is (h, k), because the graph is y = ax² translated by (h, k).

explainers.title: The Missing Corner
explainers.idea: Completing the square rewrites ax² + bx + c in vertex form by adding the missing corner of a square.

explainers.title: One More Bolt
explainers.idea: Choose the form that matches the clues, vertex or roots, and one more point fixes the value of a.

explainers.title: Two Clamps, One Centre
explainers.idea: The quadratic formula gives the roots as the axis of symmetry plus or minus a distance, which is why it has the ± sign.

explainers.title: Does It Reach the Floor?
explainers.idea: The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you whether a quadratic has two, one or no real roots before you solve it.

explainers.title: Tune k Until It Grazes
explainers.idea: Setting the discriminant to zero, positive or negative finds the values of a parameter where a line touches, cuts or misses a curve.

explainers.title: Below the Waterline
explainers.idea: Solve a quadratic inequality by finding the roots and reading from the sketch where the parabola is above or below the axis.

explainers.title: Quadratic Models on the GDC
explainers.idea: A quadratic model has one turning point, and the GDC gives its vertex, zeros and the parameters from data.

explainers.title: Multiply, Don't Add
explainers.idea: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor in each equal step of time, where linear growth adds the same amount.

explainers.title: The Curve That Never Lands
explainers.idea: The graph of a^x passes through (0, 1) and approaches a horizontal asymptote, which moves when the graph is translated.

explainers.title: What Power?
explainers.idea: A logarithm answers the question what power, so log_a b = c means a^c = b.

explainers.title: Bring Down the Exponent
explainers.idea: Taking logs of both sides brings an unknown exponent down, so a^x = b gives x = log b / log a.

explainers.title: The Mirrored Curve
explainers.idea: The graph of log_a x is the reflection of a^x in y = x, so it passes through (1, 0) and has a vertical asymptote.

explainers.title: A Quadratic in Disguise
explainers.idea: An equation such as 4^x − 5·2^x + 4 = 0 becomes a quadratic when you substitute u = 2^x.

explainers.title: Divide by Almost Nothing
explainers.idea: The graph of 1/x shoots off near x = 0 and fades towards 0 for large x, so both axes are asymptotes.

explainers.title: Find the Walls
explainers.idea: The vertical asymptote of (ax + b)/(cx + d) is where the denominator is zero, and the horizontal asymptote is y = a/c.

explainers.title: 1/x in Disguise
explainers.idea: Every (ax + b)/(cx + d) is 1/x stretched and translated, so its asymptotes are the moved axes.

explainers.title: The Level It Never Reaches
explainers.idea: In a model, a horizontal asymptote is the long-run value the quantity approaches but never reaches.

explainers.title: The Broken Conveyor
explainers.idea: f(x − a) + b moves every point of the graph by the vector (a, b), so the shape stays the same.

explainers.title: The Spring Press
explainers.idea: a·f(x) stretches a graph vertically by a, and f(bx) squashes it horizontally by the factor 1/b.

explainers.title: Flip Switches
explainers.idea: −f(x) reflects a graph in the x-axis and f(−x) reflects it in the y-axis: outside changes y and inside changes x.

explainers.title: Moves in Order
explainers.idea: When several transformations act together, the order matters, so follow each point through them one at a time.

explainers.title: Power and Variation Models
explainers.idea: In direct and inverse variation, y = kxⁿ, and one pair of values fixes the constant k.

explainers.title: Cubic Models
explainers.idea: A cubic model can rise, fall and rise again, and the GDC finds its turning points and fits it to data.

explainers.title: Which Model Fits?
explainers.idea: Pick a model from the shape of the data and the story, then test it against values it was not built from.

explainers.title: Fit It, Then Use It
explainers.idea: Find a model's parameters from given points or by regression, then use it only on a domain where it makes sense.

explainers.title: Half-Life and Decay
explainers.idea: Exponential decay halves the amount in every half-life, so N = N₀(½)^(t/h) and logs find the time.

explainers.title: Logarithmic Models
explainers.idea: A logarithmic model y = a + b ln x keeps growing but ever more slowly, which suits quantities like loudness or learning.

explainers.title: Growth with a Ceiling
explainers.idea: A logistic model starts like exponential growth and levels off at a carrying capacity L.

explainers.title: Piecewise Models
explainers.idea: A piecewise model uses a different rule on each part of the domain, and the pieces join up when the model is continuous.

explainers.title: Logarithmic Scales
explainers.idea: On a log scale each equal step multiplies the value by the same factor, so huge ranges fit on one axis.

explainers.title: Straighten the Data
explainers.idea: Taking logs turns an exponential relationship into a straight line on a semi-log plot and a power law into one on a log-log plot.

explainers.title: Factor and Remainder Theorems
explainers.idea: The remainder when p(x) is divided by (x − a) is p(a), so (x − a) is a factor exactly when p(a) = 0.

explainers.title: Factorise and Sketch Polynomials
explainers.idea: Once a factor is found, divide it out and repeat, and the factors give the roots and the shape of the graph.

explainers.title: Sum and Product of Roots
explainers.idea: The coefficients of a polynomial give the sum and the product of its roots without solving it.

explainers.title: Quadratic over Linear, Linear over Quadratic
explainers.idea: For a rational function, vertical asymptotes are the zeros of the denominator and the degrees decide the horizontal asymptote.

explainers.title: Slanted Asymptotes
explainers.idea: When the numerator has degree one more than the denominator, division gives a slanted asymptote the graph approaches.

explainers.title: Odd and Even Functions
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: An even function satisfies f(−x) = f(x) and is symmetric in the y-axis, and an odd function satisfies f(−x) = −f(x) and has rotational symmetry about the origin.

explainers.title: Self-Inverse Functions
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: A self-inverse function is its own inverse, so its graph is symmetric in the line y = x.

explainers.title: Restrict, Then Invert
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Choose the largest domain on which a function is one-to-one, and the graphs of f and f⁻¹ then meet on the line y = x.

explainers.title: Polynomial Inequalities
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Find where f(x) = g(x), then a sketch or a sign table shows on which intervals f(x) ≥ g(x).

explainers.title: Rational Inequalities
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Never multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign you do not know; bring everything to one side and use a sign table instead.

explainers.title: The Modulus Graphs
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: y = |f(x)| reflects the parts below the x-axis upwards, and y = f(|x|) copies the right half of the graph onto the left.

explainers.title: Graphs of 1/f(x) and [f(x)]²
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: The graph of 1/f(x) has asymptotes where f is zero and turning points where f does, and squaring makes every height positive.

explainers.title: The Graph of f(ax + b)
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: f(ax + b) is a translation followed by a horizontal stretch, and the order is fixed by how the input is built.

explainers.title: Modulus Equations and Inequalities
explainers.cluster: Symmetry, inverses, inequalities and modulus (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Solve |f(x)| = g(x) by taking each sign of the modulus in turn and checking every answer against the graph.

explainers.title: An Angle Fixes a Ratio
explainers.idea: In similar right-angled triangles the ratios of sides depend only on the angle, which gives sine, cosine and tangent.

explainers.title: The Sine Rule
explainers.idea: In any triangle each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same value.

explainers.title: The Cosine Rule
explainers.idea: The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction term, and it finds a side from two sides and the angle between them or an angle from three sides.

explainers.title: Half ab sin C
explainers.idea: The area of a triangle is ½ab sin C, because b sin C is the height above the side a.

explainers.title: Angles in the Field
explainers.idea: Angles of elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal and bearings clockwise from north, so draw the diagram before choosing a ratio.

explainers.title: Two Triangles, One Answer
explainers.idea: Split a problem into triangles that share a side, solve the one with enough information first and carry the shared side across.

explainers.title: Distance and Midpoint in 3D
explainers.idea: Distance in 3D is Pythagoras applied twice, √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²), and the midpoint averages each coordinate.

explainers.title: Volume and Surface Area of Solids
explainers.idea: Use the volume and surface area formulae for pyramids, cones and spheres, and add or subtract parts for combined solids.

explainers.title: Angles in 3D
explainers.idea: To find an angle in a solid, find a right-angled triangle inside it that contains the angle.

explainers.title: A Slice of the Circle
explainers.idea: An arc and a sector are the fraction θ/360 of the whole circumference and the whole area.
explainers.note: Shared core: AI SL works in degrees, and the radian explainers build on this one.

explainers.title: Radians
explainers.idea: A radian is the angle that cuts off an arc equal to the radius, so a full turn is 2π radians.

explainers.title: Arcs and Sectors in Radians
explainers.idea: In radians the arc length is rθ and the sector area is ½r²θ, because θ/2π of the circle is taken.

explainers.title: Segments and Shaded Regions
explainers.idea: A segment is a sector with its triangle removed, and other shaded regions are built by adding and subtracting such pieces.

explainers.title: Sector from Two Conditions
explainers.idea: When the perimeter and the area of a sector are both given, the two formulae become simultaneous equations in r and θ.

explainers.title: Equally Far from Both
explainers.idea: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and B, and it passes through the midpoint at right angles.

explainers.title: Voronoi Diagrams
explainers.idea: A Voronoi diagram splits the plane into cells of points closest to each site, with edges on perpendicular bisectors.

explainers.title: Using a Voronoi Diagram
explainers.idea: Edge equations, cell areas and the point furthest from every site, the toxic waste dump problem, all come from the bisectors.

explainers.title: The Unit Circle
explainers.idea: On the unit circle a point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), which defines sine and cosine for any angle.

explainers.title: Exact Values
explainers.idea: The 45° and 30–60° triangles give exact values such as sin(π/6) = ½ and cos(π/4) = √2/2.

explainers.title: Related Angles and the Quadrants
explainers.idea: Angles symmetric on the unit circle share a ratio up to sign, so one acute angle gives the values in all four quadrants.

explainers.title: The Ambiguous Case
explainers.idea: Because sin θ = sin(180° − θ), the sine rule can give two possible triangles, and both may fit the information.

explainers.title: cos² + sin² = 1
explainers.idea: Pythagoras on the unit circle gives cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, so one ratio and a quadrant give the others.

explainers.title: Double-Angle Identities
explainers.idea: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos 2θ has three forms, and choosing the right form is the skill.

explainers.title: Proving Trig Identities
explainers.idea: Prove a trigonometric identity like any other: start on one side and rewrite it using known identities until it becomes the other.

explainers.title: Reading a Wave
explainers.idea: For a sinusoidal wave the amplitude is half the height from minimum to maximum, the principal axis is halfway between them and the period is the length of one cycle.
explainers.note: Shared core: AI SL meets sinusoidal models in degrees in topic 2; the AA explainers build on it with radians.

explainers.title: Transforming sin and cos
explainers.idea: a sin(b(x − c)) + d is sin x stretched and translated, so a, b, c and d set the amplitude, period, phase and axis.

explainers.title: Find the Wave's Equation
explainers.idea: Read the maximum, minimum and period from a graph or a context to find a, b, c and d.

explainers.title: Trig Equations on the GDC
explainers.idea: Graph both sides over the given interval and read every intersection, since a trigonometric equation has many solutions.

explainers.title: Every Solution in the Interval
explainers.idea: Find one solution, use the symmetry of the unit circle to find its partner, then add whole periods to collect every solution in the interval.

explainers.title: Equations Like sin 2x = k
explainers.idea: For sin(bx + c) = k, solve for the whole argument over a stretched interval first, then undo to find x.

explainers.title: Quadratics in sin and cos
explainers.idea: Use an identity to write the equation in one ratio, solve the quadratic, and factorise instead of dividing so no solution is lost.

explainers.title: sec, cosec and cot
explainers.idea: sec, cosec and cot are the reciprocals of cos, sin and tan, and dividing cos² + sin² = 1 gives two new Pythagorean identities.

explainers.title: Using the New Identities
explainers.idea: Rewrite expressions with 1 + tan² = sec² or 1 + cot² = cosec² to simplify, prove and solve.

explainers.title: arcsin, arccos and arctan
explainers.idea: The inverse trigonometric functions undo sin, cos and tan on a restricted domain, so they return only one angle.

explainers.title: Compound Angle Formulae
explainers.idea: sin(A ± B) and cos(A ± B) expand into products of the separate ratios, which gives exact values for angles like 75°.

explainers.title: Doubles from Compounds
explainers.idea: Setting A = B in the compound formulae gives the double-angle identities, including tan 2θ.

explainers.title: Symmetries of the Trig Graphs
explainers.idea: cos is even and sin is odd, and shifting by π/2 turns one into the other, which explains every related-angle identity.

explainers.title: Solutions from Symmetry
explainers.idea: The symmetry of a trigonometric graph gives the other solutions of an equation from the first one.

explainers.title: Vectors and Components
explainers.idea: A vector says how far to move in each direction, and vectors add component by component and have a length called the magnitude.

explainers.title: Parallel and Collinear
explainers.idea: Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other, and three points are collinear when two of the vectors between them are parallel.

explainers.title: Proofs with Vectors
explainers.idea: Divide a line in a ratio and prove geometric facts by expressing every vector in terms of two base vectors.

explainers.title: The Scalar Product
explainers.idea: a · b multiplies matching components and adds them, equals |a||b| cos θ and is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular.

explainers.title: Properties of the Scalar Product
explainers.idea: The scalar product is commutative and distributes over addition, and a · a = |a|², which makes vector algebra work like expanding brackets.

explainers.title: The Vector Product
explainers.idea: a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b, with magnitude |a||b| sin θ.

explainers.title: Areas from the Vector Product
explainers.idea: The magnitude of a × b is the area of the parallelogram the vectors span, and half of it is the area of the triangle.

explainers.title: The Vector Equation of a Line
explainers.idea: r = a + λb reaches every point on a line by starting at a and moving any multiple of the direction b.

explainers.title: The Angle Between Two Lines
explainers.idea: The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors, found with the scalar product.

explainers.title: Motion with Constant Velocity
explainers.idea: A position r = a + tv is a line where the parameter is time and the direction is the velocity.

explainers.title: Closest Approach
explainers.idea: Two objects are closest when the vector between them is perpendicular to their relative motion, and they collide only if they are at the same point at the same time.

explainers.title: Variable Velocity in the Plane
explainers.idea: When velocity changes with time, differentiate or integrate each component separately to move between position, velocity and acceleration.

explainers.title: Do Two Lines Meet?
explainers.idea: Two lines meet if one pair of parameter values satisfies all three component equations; otherwise they are parallel or skew.

explainers.title: Skew Lines
explainers.idea: Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting, which happens only in three dimensions.

explainers.title: The Equation of a Plane
explainers.idea: A plane is fixed by a point and a normal vector n, giving r · n = a · n, or ax + by + cz = d in Cartesian form.

explainers.title: Planes from Conditions
explainers.idea: Three points, or a line and a point, give two direction vectors in the plane, and their vector product is the normal.

explainers.title: Where a Line Meets a Plane
explainers.idea: Substitute the line's parametric form into the plane's equation to find the parameter at the point where they meet.

explainers.title: Where Planes Meet
explainers.idea: Two planes meet in a line, and three planes meet in a point, a line or nowhere, which is a system of three equations.

explainers.title: Angles with Planes
explainers.idea: Angles involving planes use the normal vector, so the angle between a line and a plane is 90° minus the angle with the normal.

explainers.title: Matrices Move the Plane
explainers.idea: The columns of a 2 × 2 matrix are where the unit vectors go, which fixes a rotation, reflection, stretch or enlargement.

explainers.title: Combining Transformations
explainers.idea: Doing transformation A then B is the matrix BA, and the determinant is the factor that multiplies every area.

explainers.title: Vertices and Edges
explainers.idea: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges, and the degree of a vertex counts the edges that meet it.

explainers.title: Adjacency Matrices and Walks
explainers.idea: The entries of Aᵏ count the walks of length k between each pair of vertices.

explainers.title: Random Walks on a Graph
explainers.idea: Scaling each column of an adjacency matrix to add to 1 gives a transition matrix for a random walk on the graph.

explainers.title: Eulerian Trails and the Chinese Postman
explainers.idea: A route that uses every edge once exists when the odd vertices number zero or two, and the Chinese postman repeats the cheapest pairing of odd vertices.

explainers.title: Minimum Spanning Trees
explainers.idea: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms connect every vertex at the least total cost by adding the cheapest edge that makes no cycle.

explainers.title: The Travelling Salesman
explainers.idea: The best cycle through every vertex is hard to find, so trap its length between an upper bound from nearest neighbour and a lower bound from a spanning tree.

explainers.title: Who You Ask Matters
explainers.idea: A sample stands in for a population only if it is chosen fairly, by a method such as simple random, systematic, stratified or quota sampling.

explainers.title: Types of Data and Bias
explainers.idea: Data are discrete or continuous, and bias in how they are collected or which outliers are dropped changes what they can show.

explainers.title: Designing a Data Collection
explainers.idea: Good questions and well-chosen variables make data valid, and repeating a measurement checks that it is reliable.

explainers.title: Histograms
explainers.idea: A histogram shows grouped continuous data as bars with no gaps, whose heights are the frequencies.

explainers.title: Cumulative Frequency
explainers.idea: A cumulative frequency graph plots the running total against upper class boundaries, so the median and quartiles are read across from the right heights.

explainers.title: Box Plots and Outliers
explainers.idea: A box plot draws the five-number summary, a value more than 1.5 IQR beyond a quartile is an outlier, and two plots compare centre and spread.

explainers.title: Mean, Median and Mode
explainers.idea: The mean shares the total equally, the median is the middle value and the mode is the most common, and outliers decide which suits the data.

explainers.title: Quartiles and Standard Deviation
explainers.idea: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle half, and the standard deviation measures the typical distance from the mean.

explainers.title: Shift and Scale the Data
explainers.idea: Adding a constant to every value moves the centre but not the spread, while multiplying scales both.

explainers.title: Unbiased Estimates
explainers.idea: The sample mean estimates the population mean, but the variance needs dividing by n − 1 to be unbiased.

explainers.title: Correlation and r
explainers.idea: Pearson's r measures how close points lie to a straight line, from −1 to 1, and correlation is not causation.

explainers.title: The Line of Best Fit
explainers.idea: The regression line of y on x passes through the mean point and predicts y from x, but only within the data.

explainers.title: The Other Regression Line
explainers.idea: To predict x from y use the regression line of x on y, and the two lines cross at the mean point.

explainers.title: Spearman's Rank
explainers.idea: Spearman's coefficient is Pearson's r applied to the ranks, so it measures whether the relationship always goes the same way.

explainers.title: Pearson or Spearman?
explainers.idea: Use Pearson for a linear relationship and Spearman for a monotonic one, and notice how an outlier affects each.

explainers.title: Non-Linear Regression
explainers.idea: The GDC fits quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and sine models by least squares, and the scatter plot suggests which to try.

explainers.title: How Good Is the Fit?
explainers.idea: The residuals measure how far the data are from a model, and R² is the share of the variation the model explains.

explainers.title: Equally Likely Outcomes
explainers.idea: When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes over the total, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

explainers.title: Probability in the Long Run
explainers.idea: A relative frequency estimates a probability, and n × P(A) is the number of times you expect A in n trials.

explainers.title: Venn Diagrams
explainers.idea: A Venn diagram shows overlapping events, and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) avoids counting the overlap twice.

explainers.title: Trees and Sample Spaces
explainers.idea: Multiply along the branches of a tree and add the paths you want, or count the cells of a sample-space grid.

explainers.title: Given That
explainers.idea: Given that B happened, B becomes the whole sample space, so P(A | B) is the part of B that is also A.

explainers.title: Independent Events
explainers.idea: Events are independent when knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other.

explainers.title: The Conditional Probability Formula
explainers.idea: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), which also gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B) for building trees backwards.

explainers.title: Testing for Independence
explainers.idea: A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), which tests independence or finds a missing probability.

explainers.title: Bayes' Theorem
explainers.idea: Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability, which is why a positive test for a rare condition is often a false alarm.

explainers.title: Random Variables
explainers.idea: A discrete random variable lists every value with its probability, and the probabilities add to 1.

explainers.title: Expected Value
explainers.idea: E(X) is the long-run average, the sum of each value times its probability, and a game is fair when the expected gain is zero.

explainers.title: Is It Binomial?
explainers.idea: A count of successes is binomial when there is a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same chance of success.

explainers.title: Binomial Probabilities
explainers.idea: P(X = r) counts the paths with r successes and multiplies by the probability of each, and the GDC gives exact and cumulative values.
explainers.note: Shared by all four courses, so nCr from the binomial theorem (AA only) is a callback, not a prerequisite.

explainers.title: Mean and Variance of a Binomial
explainers.idea: For X ~ B(n, p) the mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p), which can also find n or p.

explainers.title: The Poisson Distribution
explainers.idea: A Poisson variable counts random events at a constant average rate, with mean and variance both equal to the rate.

explainers.title: Using the Poisson Model
explainers.idea: Independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count, and the context decides between Poisson and binomial.

explainers.title: The Bell Curve
explainers.idea: A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, and about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations.

explainers.title: Normal Probabilities
explainers.idea: A normal probability is the area under the curve between two values, found on the GDC.

explainers.title: Inverse Normal
explainers.idea: The inverse normal turns an area back into the value that cuts it off, so draw which side the area is on first.

explainers.title: Standardising
explainers.idea: z = (x − μ)/σ counts how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, which compares values from different distributions.

explainers.title: Finding μ or σ
explainers.idea: When μ or σ is unknown, standardise and use the inverse normal to write an equation for each given probability.

explainers.title: Scaling a Random Variable
explainers.idea: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), because adding moves the distribution and multiplying stretches it.

explainers.title: Variance of a Discrete Variable
explainers.idea: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]², the average squared distance from the mean.

explainers.title: Probability Density Functions
explainers.idea: For a continuous variable, probability is the area under the density function, and the total area is 1.

explainers.title: Mean, Median and Mode of a pdf
explainers.idea: The mean of a pdf is ∫x f(x) dx, the median splits the area in half and the mode is where the density peaks.

explainers.title: Combining Random Variables
explainers.idea: Means of independent variables add and subtract, but their variances always add.

explainers.title: Adding Normal Variables
explainers.idea: A sum of independent normal variables is normal, and X₁ + X₂ differs from 2X because the variances behave differently.

explainers.title: The Central Limit Theorem
explainers.idea: The mean of a large sample is approximately normal with standard deviation σ/√n, whatever the shape of the population.

explainers.title: Confidence Intervals
explainers.idea: A confidence interval is a range built so that, in repeated samples, a set percentage of such ranges contain the true mean.

explainers.title: Hypotheses and p-Values
explainers.idea: Assume the null hypothesis, and reject it only if data this extreme would be rare, that is if the p-value is below the significance level.

explainers.title: χ² Test for Independence
explainers.idea: Compare observed counts in a table with the counts expected under independence, and a large χ² is evidence of a link.

explainers.title: χ² Goodness of Fit
explainers.idea: A goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts with those a model predicts.

explainers.title: Degrees of Freedom and Merged Cells
explainers.idea: Merge categories with expected counts below 5 and lose a degree of freedom for each parameter estimated from the data.

explainers.title: The t-Test
explainers.idea: A two-sample t-test asks whether two sample means differ by more than chance would explain.

explainers.title: Critical Regions and Errors
explainers.idea: The critical region is the set of results that lead to rejection, and a type I error rejects a true null while a type II error keeps a false one.

explainers.title: Testing a Mean
explainers.idea: Test a population mean with the distribution of the sample mean, using z when σ is known and t when it is estimated.

explainers.title: Testing a Proportion or a Rate
explainers.idea: Test a proportion with a binomial model and a rate with a Poisson model, adding up the tail probabilities.

explainers.title: Testing a Correlation
explainers.idea: Test whether a population correlation is zero by comparing the sample's r with its p-value.

explainers.title: Transition Matrices
explainers.idea: A transition matrix holds the probabilities of moving between states, and multiplying by it n times gives the state after n steps.

explainers.title: The Steady State
explainers.idea: A regular chain settles into a steady state that the transition matrix leaves unchanged, found by high powers or by solving equations.

explainers.title: From Chord to Tangent
explainers.idea: As the second point slides towards the first, the gradient of the chord approaches a limit, the gradient of the tangent.

explainers.title: The Derivative as a Rate
explainers.idea: f′(x) is the gradient of the curve at x, the rate at which the output changes per unit of input, with units to match.

explainers.title: The Power Rule
explainers.idea: The derivative of axⁿ is naxⁿ⁻¹, so rewrite roots and fractions as powers first.

explainers.title: Gradient at a Point
explainers.idea: Substitute x into f′(x) to get the gradient there, or set f′(x) equal to a value to find where the gradient is that value.

explainers.title: Uphill and Downhill
explainers.idea: A function increases where f′(x) > 0 and decreases where f′(x) < 0.

explainers.title: Always Increasing
explainers.idea: Show a function always increases by showing f′(x) > 0 for every x, often by completing the square or using the discriminant.

explainers.title: Tangents and Normals
explainers.idea: The tangent at a point has gradient f′(a), and the normal is the line through the same point perpendicular to it.

explainers.title: Tangents That Meet Things
explainers.idea: Find where a tangent meets an axis or the curve again, or what makes a line a tangent, by combining the tangent equation with the curve.

explainers.title: Derivatives of eˣ, ln x, sin x and cos x
explainers.idea: eˣ is its own derivative, ln x has derivative 1/x, and sin and cos differentiate into each other in radians.

explainers.title: The Chain Rule
explainers.idea: To differentiate a composite, differentiate the outer function and multiply by the derivative of the inner one.

explainers.title: The Product Rule
explainers.idea: The derivative of uv is u′v + uv′: each factor changes while the other holds still.

explainers.title: The Quotient Rule
explainers.idea: The derivative of u/v is (u′v − uv′)/v², which is the product rule applied to u × v⁻¹.

explainers.title: Using the Rules with Values
explainers.idea: With values of f, g and their derivatives at a point, the rules give the derivative of a combination at that point without its formula.

explainers.title: Show That the Derivative Is…
explainers.idea: When asked to show a derivative has a given form, differentiate, then factorise and simplify towards the target.

explainers.title: Where the Gradient Is Zero
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: At a local maximum or minimum the tangent is horizontal, so solve f′(x) = 0 to find it.

explainers.title: Maximum or Minimum?
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: If f′ changes from positive to negative the point is a maximum, and from negative to positive a minimum.

explainers.title: Greatest and Least on an Interval
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: On a closed interval the greatest and least values are at stationary points or at the endpoints, so check both.

explainers.title: Optimising a Given Model
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: To optimise a model, find where its derivative is zero, check the type and the domain, and answer in context.

explainers.title: Build the Model, Then Optimise
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: Use the constraint to write the quantity in one variable, then optimise it.

explainers.title: Stationary Points with Unknowns
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: A given stationary point gives two equations, f(a) = b and f′(a) = 0, to find unknown coefficients.

explainers.title: The Second Derivative
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: f″(x) is the derivative of the derivative, the rate at which the gradient changes.

explainers.title: Concave Up, Concave Down
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: A curve is concave up where f″ > 0, bending like a cup, and concave down where f″ < 0.

explainers.title: The Second Derivative Test
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: At a stationary point, f″ > 0 means a minimum and f″ < 0 a maximum, and f″ = 0 tells you nothing.

explainers.title: Points of Inflexion
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: A point of inflexion is where the concavity changes, so f″ = 0 there and changes sign.

explainers.title: Graphs of f, f′ and f″
explainers.cluster: Second derivative, stationary points and optimisation
explainers.idea: The zeros of f′ are the turning points of f and the zeros of f″ its inflexions, so each graph can be read from the other.

explainers.title: Velocity and Acceleration
explainers.idea: Velocity is the derivative of displacement and acceleration the derivative of velocity, and a particle is at rest when v = 0.

explainers.title: Displacement or Distance?
explainers.idea: Integrating velocity gives the change in displacement, but distance travelled integrates |v|, so split where the particle turns.

explainers.title: Speed and Motion Graphs
explainers.idea: Speed is |v|, so maximum speed can come from the most negative velocity, and the graph of v shows it all.

explainers.title: Undo the Derivative
explainers.idea: Integration reverses differentiation, so ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, and a known point fixes C.

explainers.title: The Area Under a Curve
explainers.idea: The definite integral adds up thin strips to give the area between a curve above the axis and the x-axis, and the GDC evaluates it.

explainers.title: Rate In, Total Out
explainers.idea: Integrating a rate of change over an interval gives the total change in the quantity.

explainers.title: The Trapezoidal Rule
explainers.idea: Split the area into strips of equal width and treat each as a trapezium to approximate the integral.

explainers.title: Over or Under?
explainers.idea: Trapezia overestimate the area under a curve that bends up and underestimate it under one that bends down.

explainers.title: Integrals of eˣ, 1/x, sin and cos
explainers.idea: Read the derivatives backwards: ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C, and sin and cos integrate into each other.

explainers.title: Integrating f(ax + b)
explainers.idea: To integrate a function of ax + b, integrate as usual and divide by a, undoing the chain rule.

explainers.title: Spot the Derivative Inside
explainers.idea: When an integrand contains a function and its derivative, the integral reverses the chain rule, by inspection or by substitution.

explainers.title: Rewrite, Then Integrate
explainers.idea: Expand, split fractions or use an identity until each term has a standard integral.

explainers.title: Find f from f′
explainers.idea: Integrate the derivative and use a known point to find the constant, and a hence part often hands you the derivative to reverse.

explainers.title: Evaluating Definite Integrals
explainers.idea: Evaluate F(b) − F(a) with the antiderivative, and use the properties to split, reverse or scale an integral.

explainers.title: Area Below the Axis
explainers.idea: An integral counts area below the axis as negative, so split at the roots or integrate |f(x)| to find total area.

explainers.title: Area Between Two Curves
explainers.idea: The area between two curves integrates the top minus the bottom between their intersections.

explainers.title: Unknown Limits and Parameters
explainers.idea: When an integral's value is given, evaluate it in terms of the unknown and solve the equation.

explainers.title: Area Against the y-Axis
explainers.idea: For area against the y-axis, write x as a function of y and integrate with respect to y.

explainers.title: Volume of Revolution About the x-Axis
explainers.idea: Spinning a curve about the x-axis makes discs of area πy², so the volume is ∫πy² dx.

explainers.title: Volume of Revolution About the y-Axis
explainers.idea: About the y-axis the discs have area πx², so write x² in terms of y and integrate with respect to y.

explainers.title: Volumes Between Two Curves
explainers.idea: The solid between two curves is the outer volume minus the inner one, π∫(y₁² − y₂²) dx, not π∫(y₁ − y₂)² dx.

explainers.title: Continuity and Differentiability
explainers.idea: A function is continuous where its graph has no break and differentiable where it also has no corner.

explainers.title: Differentiation from First Principles
explainers.idea: The derivative is the limit of (f(x + h) − f(x))/h as h tends to 0, which proves the power rule.

explainers.title: Higher Derivatives
explainers.idea: Keep differentiating to spot a pattern for the nth derivative, then prove it by induction.

explainers.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
explainers.idea: For a limit of the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, the limit of f/g equals the limit of f′/g′.

explainers.title: Limits by Maclaurin Series
explainers.idea: Replace each function by its Maclaurin series, cancel the leading powers, and the limit can be read off.

explainers.title: Implicit Differentiation
explainers.idea: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x, so every y term gains a dy/dx.

explainers.title: Related Rates
explainers.idea: When quantities are linked by an equation, the chain rule links their rates of change over time.

explainers.title: Further Standard Derivatives
explainers.idea: The derivatives of sec, cosec, cot, aˣ, log_a x and the inverse trig functions follow from the rules and the inverse relationship.

explainers.title: Further Standard Integrals
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Reversing the further derivatives gives arctan and arcsin integrals, reached by completing the square or splitting into partial fractions.

explainers.title: Integration by Substitution
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Change the variable to simplify an integral, converting dx and, for a definite integral, the limits too.

explainers.title: Integration by Parts
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫u v′ dx = uv − ∫u′v dx, choosing u to get simpler when differentiated.

explainers.title: Which Integration Technique?
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Look at the integrand's structure, a derivative inside, a product or a rational function, to pick inspection, substitution, parts or partial fractions.

explainers.title: Maclaurin Series
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: A Maclaurin series matches a function's value and every derivative at 0 with a polynomial that goes on forever.

explainers.title: Building New Series
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Substitute into, multiply, differentiate or integrate known series instead of finding every derivative.

explainers.title: Series from a Differential Equation
explainers.cluster: Further integration and Maclaurin series (AA HL)
explainers.idea: Repeatedly differentiate a differential equation to find the derivatives at 0, and so the Maclaurin series of its solution.

explainers.title: Writing a Differential Equation
explainers.idea: A sentence like the rate of growth is proportional to the size becomes dy/dt = ky.

explainers.title: Separating the Variables
explainers.idea: Gather the y terms with dy and the x terms with dx, integrate both sides and use the initial condition to find the constant.

explainers.title: Euler's Method
explainers.idea: Euler's method follows the tangent for a small step, again and again, to approximate the solution curve.

explainers.title: The Logistic Equation
explainers.idea: Separating the logistic equation needs partial fractions, and the solution levels off at the carrying capacity.

explainers.title: Homogeneous Equations
explainers.idea: The substitution y = vx turns a homogeneous equation dy/dx = f(y/x) into a separable one.

explainers.title: The Integrating Factor
explainers.idea: Multiplying dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) by e^∫P dx turns the left side into the derivative of a product.

explainers.title: Slope Fields
explainers.idea: A slope field draws a short tangent at each point, so solution curves can be sketched by following the slopes.

explainers.title: Coupled Systems
explainers.idea: When two quantities change each other, step both forward together with Euler's method.

explainers.title: Exact Solutions with Eigenvalues
explainers.idea: For a coupled linear system the eigenvalues of its matrix give the exact solution and decide whether it grows, decays or spirals.

explainers.title: Phase Portraits
explainers.idea: A phase portrait plots one variable against the other, and its shape near the origin shows the long-term behaviour.

explainers.title: Second-Order Equations
explainers.idea: A second-order equation becomes a coupled first-order system by letting the velocity be a second variable.
